claims.source: In a cell approaching completion of cytokinesis, GpsB-GFP collapsed into a single focus at the center of the invaginating membrane (Figure 3Biii), and immediately after the completion of cell division, we observed that GpsB-GFP localized largely to the cell periphery in the adjacent daughter cells (Figure 3Biv), suggesting that GpsB may dynamically localize during the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structured illumination microscopy shown in Figure 3Biii.

claims.claim: GpsB dynamically localizes during the cell cycle in S. aureus.
claims.source: To test the dynamic nature of GpsB-GFP localization, we followed the fate of GpsB-GFP in individual cells through three rounds of cell division using diffraction-limited epifluorescence microscopy.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: GpsB localization to mid-cell depends directly or indirectly on functional FtsZ.
claims.source: In the absence of inhibitor, GpsB-GFP localized at mid-cell or the periphery in 55% or 30% of cells, respectively, and mis-localized in the cytosol in 15% of cells (n = 200; Figure 4E–E'). In contrast, in the presence of inhibitor, GpsB did not localize to mid-cell in any cell observed (n = 200) and instead displayed a combination of diffuse cytosolic localization and aggregation along the cell periphery (Figure 4F–F'). The data therefore indicated that that GpsB localization to mid-cell depends directly or indirectly on functional FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy with FtsZ inhibitor PC190723 shown in Figure 4E-F'.

claims.claim: Overproduction of GpsB disrupts divisome assembly in S. aureus.
claims.source: In otherwise wild type cells producing ZapA-GFP, no cell enlargement was detected; among them, 53% of cells displayed ZapA-GFP localized to mid-cell (these were cells that were actively undergoing cell division (Figure 4G–G', arrow) and 37% of cells displayed ZapA-GFP as a ring that corresponded to the subsequent plane of cell division in daughter cells that had recently completed cytokinesis (Figure 4G–G', arrowhead; n = 200). In contrast, in cells harboring inducible gpsB, addition of inducer resulted in the enlargement of cells and ZapA-GFP was mis-localized in 86% of the enlarged cells (n = 100; Figure 4H–I').
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy of ZapA-GFP localization shown in Figure 4G-I'.

claims.claim: Depletion of GpsB prevents robust divisome assembly at mid-cell in S. aureus.
claims.source: In cells harboring empty vector, ZapA-GFP localized to mid-cell in 82.5% of the cells (n = 200; Figure 4J–J'). Quantification of fluorescence intensity in individual cells revealed that the fluorescence of mid-cell-localized ZapA-GFP was 2429 ± 1346 units/cell (n = 75). At earlier time points after induction to deplete GpsB, before cell lysis, we observed faint ZapA-GFP signals at mid-cell in 41% of the cells and diffuse localization in the remaining cells (n = 200; Figure 4K–K'), but the mean fluorescence intensity of the ZapA-GFP ring structure (614 ± 450 units/cell; n = 75) was nearly four-fold lower than that observed for ZapA-GFP intensity in the absence of gpsB depletion.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy and fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4J-K'.

claims.claim: S. aureus GpsB elutes in two peaks by size exclusion chromatography, corresponding to hexameric and dodecameric forms.
claims.source: GpsB eluted in two peaks by size exclusion chromatography, which approximately corresponds to the predicted sizes of hexameric (Rismondo et al., 2016) and dodecameric GpsB (Figure 5B, top), indicating that S. aureus GpsB could potentially exist in two forms.
claims.evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: GpsB-L35S elutes exclusively as a dodecamer by size exclusion chromatography.
claims.source: In contrast, GpsBL35S eluted exclusively as a dodecamer (Figure 5B, bottom), suggesting that its inability to form hexamers could underlie its loss of function in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: S. aureus FtsZ hydrolyzed GTP poorly below ~30 μM.
claims.source: Unlike the well-characterized E. coli FtsZ, which robustly hydrolyzes GTP (Arjes et al., 2015; Buske and Levin, 2012; Mukherjee and Lutkenhaus, 1998; Romberg and Levin, 2003), S. aureus FtsZ hydrolyzed GTP poorly below ~30 μM (Figure 5C) (Anderson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The rate of GTP hydrolysis by S. aureus FtsZ continued to increase with FtsZ concentration.
claims.source: The rate of hydrolysis continued to increase with FtsZ concentration (Figure 5D), displaying a behavior more similar to FtsZ from the Gram-positive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which has a critical concentration above 10 µM, than to E. coli FtsZ (although a lag observed for S. pneumonia FtsZ was not detected for S. aureus FtsZ) (Salvarelli et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis rate measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Incubation of 30 µM FtsZ with increasing amounts of GpsB resulted in a non-linear stimulation of GTP hydrolysis activity.
claims.source: Incubation of 30 µM FtsZ with increasing amounts of GpsB resulted in a non-linear stimulation of GTP hydrolysis activity, wherein appreciable stimulation of GTP hydrolysis was only seen above 8 μM GpsB (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: At 10 µM GpsB, GTP hydrolysis by FtsZ was stimulated ~3 fold.
claims.source: At 10 µM GpsB (1:3 ratio of monomeric GpsB:FtsZ; 1:18 ratio of hexameric GpsB:FtsZ; 1:36 ratio of dodecameric GpsB:FtsZ), GTP hydrolysis was stimulated ~3 fold.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: GpsB alone does not exhibit appreciable GTPase activity.
claims.source: As a control, GpsB alone did not exhibit appreciable GTPase activity (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Incubation of FtsZ with GpsB-L35S did not appreciably stimulate GTPase activity of FtsZ.
claims.source: In contrast, incubation of FtsZ with GpsBL35S did not appreciably stimulate GTPase activity of FtsZ (Figure 5F), nor did the addition of GpsB, even at equimolar amounts, to lower concentrations (10 µM) of FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Wild type GpsB stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ at substoichiometric levels at sufficiently high concentrations of FtsZ (above 30 μM).
claims.source: Thus, wild type GpsB, which purifies as a hexamer and dodecamer, stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ at substoichiometric levels at sufficiently high enough concentrations of FtsZ (above 30 μM), whereas GpsBL35S, which is locked in the dodecameric form, fails to do so.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the GTP hydrolysis and size exclusion chromatography data.

claims.claim: In the presence of GMPCPP, more than 50% of FtsZ was detected in the pellet fraction after ultracentrifugation.
claims.source: In the absence of nucleotide, FtsZ was largely detected in the supernatant after ultracentrifugation, but in the presence of GMPCPP, more than 50% of FtsZ was detected in the pellet fraction, indicating that it had polymerized (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: 94% of GpsB co-sedimented with FtsZ in the presence of GMPCPP.
claims.source: When GpsB was incubated with the reaction, 94% of GpsB co-sedimented with FtsZ, whereas only 20% of the nonfunctional GpsBL35S co-sedimented with FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Only 20% of GpsB-L35S co-sedimented with FtsZ in the presence of GMPCPP.
claims.source: When GpsB was incubated with the reaction, 94% of GpsB co-sedimented with FtsZ, whereas only 20% of the nonfunctional GpsBL35S co-sedimented with FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the absence of FtsZ, GpsB and GpsB-L35S were largely soluble.
claims.source: Finally, in the absence of FtsZ, GpsB and GpsBL35S were largely soluble, suggesting that GpsB, but not GpsBL35S, interacts with FtsZ polymers.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Addition of GpsB increased the fraction of FtsZ in the pellet at slower centrifugation speed.
claims.source: At a slower centrifugation speed, we detected 43% of FtsZ in the pellet fraction in the presence of GMPCPP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Addition of GpsB increased the fraction of FtsZ in the pellet to 55%, whereas addition of GpsBL35S did not significantly alter the pelleted fraction of FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential centrifugation assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In the presence of GTP, FtsZ formed linear polymers ~100 nm in length.
claims.source: In the presence of GTP, FtsZ formed linear polymers,~100 nm in length, that were abundant and scattered in different directions on the grid, indicating that it had polymerized successfully in a GTP-dependent manner (Figure 6D,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy shown in Figure 6D,H.

claims.claim: In the presence of GpsB and GTP, FtsZ polymers formed long filaments closer to 1 µm in length that were oriented in a similar direction.
claims.source: In the presence GpsB and GTP, however, FtsZ polymers formed long filaments, closer to 1 µm in length, which were oriented in a similar direction (Figure 6E,I). This pattern of orientation on an EM grid was reminiscent of the bundling behavior reported previously for proteins in E. coli that could promote lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments in vitro (Hale et al., 2000; Small et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy shown in Figure 6E,I.

claims.claim: GpsB-mediated bundling of FtsZ did not require GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: With GMPCPP, FtsZ polymers were very long and in the presence of GpsB also exhibited extensive lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments, indicating that GpsB-mediated bundling of FtsZ did not require GTP hydrolysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy with GMPCPP shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E.

claims.claim: Incubation of 10 µM or 20 µM purified S. aureus FtsZ with GTP did not result in an appreciable increase in light scattering.
claims.source: Incubation of either 10 µM or 20 µM purified S. aureus FtsZ with GTP did not result in an appreciable increase in light scattering (Figure 6J), consistent with the apparent high critical concentration for FtsZ assembly suggested in GTP turnover experiments (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by light scattering assays shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Incubation of 30 µM or 40 µM FtsZ with GTP resulted in a rapid increase in light scattering followed by a brief plateau and then a decrease.
claims.source: Incubation of 30 µM or 40 µM FtsZ with GTP resulted in a rapid increase in light scattering that likely corresponds to the assembly of FtsZ polymers. The increase was followed by a brief plateau, likely reflecting that the reaction was at steady state, then a decrease in light scattering, corresponding to disassembly of FtsZ polymers coincident with depletion of GTP in the reaction.
claims.evidence: This is supported by light scattering assays shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Addition of 10 µM GpsB to the reaction with GTP and 30 µM FtsZ resulted in an initial increase in light scattering that was much more rapid and larger in amplitude than that of FtsZ alone.
claims.source: Addition of 10 µM GpsB to the reaction with GTP and 30 µM FtsZ resulted in an initial increase in light scattering that was much more rapid and larger in amplitude than that of FtsZ alone in the presence of GTP (Figure 6K), whereas incubation of GpsB alone with GTP did not result in an increase in light scattering.
claims.evidence: This is supported by light scattering assays shown in Figure 6K.

claims.claim: The assembly of the higher order FtsZ structures generated in the presence of GpsB was reversible.
claims.source: After reaching a plateau, the reaction containing WT GpsB displayed a steady decrease in light scattering, suggesting that the assembly of the higher order FtsZ structures generated in the presence of GpsB was reversible, in contrast to the behavior of other FtsZ bundling proteins reported in other systems.
claims.evidence: This is supported by extended light scattering assays shown in Figure 6L.

claims.claim: GpsB directly interacts with polymerized FtsZ and bundles FtsZ filaments.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that GpsB directly interacts with polymerized FtsZ and bundles FtsZ filaments.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on co-sedimentation, electron microscopy, and light scattering data.

claims.claim: FtsZ bundling by GpsB increases FtsZ local concentration and triggers GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: Taken together with the observation that GpsB also triggers GTP hydrolysis by FtsZ, we propose that FtsZ bundling by GpsB increases FtsZ local concentration and triggers GTP hydrolysis which, in the light scattering assay, is linked to the disassembly of FtsZ polymers as GTP is depleted.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: Cell division in S. aureus proceeds in two principal steps: an initial FtsZ treadmilling-dependent step followed by recruitment of peptidoglycan remodeling enzymes.
claims.source: A recent report suggested that cell division in S. aureus proceeds in two principal steps: an initial FtsZ treadmilling-dependent step in which membrane invagination initiates, followed by recruitment of peptidoglycan remodeling enzymes by later arriving divisome components that mediates the progression and completion of cell division (Monteiro et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: GpsB may participate in the initial step that stabilizes FtsZ at mid-cell and activates GTP hydrolysis to trigger FtsZ treadmilling.
claims.source: We propose that GpsB may participate in the initial step that stabilizes FtsZ at mid-cell and activates GTP hydrolysis (by increasing the local concentration of FtsZ via a bundling-like mechanism) to trigger FtsZ treadmilling, which is linked to constriction of the membrane and concurrent peptidoglycan synthesis (Bisson-Filho et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claims.claim: Intracellular levels of FtsZ and GpsB in S. aureus are approximately 4452 and 1659 molecules per cell, respectively.
claims.source: Intracellular levels of FtsZ and GpsB are reported to be approximately 4452 and 1659 molecules per cell, respectively (Zühlke et al., 2016) (S. Fuchs, personal communication).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and personal communication.

claims.claim: Considering a cell diameter of 0.8 µm, intracellular concentrations of FtsZ and GpsB equate to 28 uM and 10 uM, respectively.
claims.source: Considering a cell diameter of 0.8 µm, this equates to intracellular concentrations of 28 uM FtsZ and 10 uM GpsB and corresponds closely with our in vitro reaction conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on reported molecule numbers and cell dimensions.

claims.claim: GpsB is a multimer that may harbor 6–12 binding sites per multimer to recruit and bridge multiple FtsZ proteins.
claims.source: We show that GpsB is a multimer and propose that it may harbor 6–12 binding sites per multimer to recruit and bridge multiple FtsZ proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the size exclusion chromatography data showing hexameric and dodecameric forms.

claims.claim: The bridging of FtsZ filaments by GpsB serves to increase the local FtsZ concentration and enhances GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: We propose that the bridging of FtsZ filaments also serves to increase the local FtsZ concentration and enhances GTP hydrolysis.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the bundling and GTPase stimulation data.

claims.claim: GpsB is the first reported FtsZ regulatory protein that promotes both lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments while also stimulating GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of an FtsZ regulatory protein that promotes both lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments while also stimulating GTP hydrolysis.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on comparison with known FtsZ regulators.

claims.claim: FtsZ polymers and regulators appear poised at the threshold between assembly and disassembly, enabling tight control over the division process.
claims.source: Furthermore, considering the intracellular concentrations of FtsZ and GpsB and what we have observed biochemically, FtsZ polymers and regulators appear poised at the threshold between assembly and disassembly, enabling tight control over the division process.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the biochemical data and intracellular concentrations.

claims.claim: Overexpression of gpsB resulted in the enlargement of S. aureus cells, reminiscent of the phenotype caused by depletion of FtsZ.
claims.source: First, overexpression of gpsB resulted in the enlargement of S. aureus cells, reminiscent of the phenotype caused by depletion of FtsZ (Pinho and Errington, 2003), likely due to increased FtsZ GTPase activity leading to the inability of FtsZ to polymerize and treadmill in a concerted fashion.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell size measurements and comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: Depletion of GpsB in S. aureus resulted in the arrest of cytokinesis and abrogation of initiation of cell division.
claims.source: Second, depletion of GpsB in S. aureus resulted in the arrest of cytokinesis and abrogation of initiation of cell division.
claims.evidence: This is supported by antisense RNA depletion experiments and microscopy.

claims.claim: GpsB co-localized with the cell division machinery at the onset of cytokinesis and co-constricted with the invaginating membrane during cell division.
claims.source: Third, we observed that GpsB co-localized with the cell division machinery at the onset of cytokinesis, and co-constricted with the invaginating membrane during cell division, consistent with its role in modulating the activity of FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing GpsB localization dynamics.

claims.claim: Purified GpsB directly interacted with FtsZ in vitro and stimulated the GTPase activity of FtsZ.
claims.source: Fourth, we found that purified GpsB directly interacted with FtsZ in vitro and stimulated the GTPase activity of FtsZ, consistent with the ability of GpsB to inhibit cell division in vivo when overproduced.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation and GTP hydrolysis assays.

claims.claim: When incubated with FtsZ in vitro, GpsB promoted lateral interactions between FtsZ polymers but also allowed for the ultimate disassembly of FtsZ once GTP had been depleted.
claims.source: Finally, when incubated with FtsZ in vitro, GpsB promoted lateral interactions between FtsZ polymers, but also allowed for the ultimate disassembly of FtsZ in vitro once GTP had been depleted.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and light scattering assays.

claims.claim: Staphylococcal FtsZ begins assembling at mid-cell and recruits GpsB to that location.
claims.source: Our genetic, cytological, and biochemical data in sum suggest a model in which Staphylococcal FtsZ begins assembling at mid-cell and recruits GpsB to that location (Figure 7B) where GpsB stabilizes the Z-ring via a bundling-like mechanism that concentrates and organizes FtsZ polymers.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on integration of multiple experimental observations and shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: GpsB stabilizes the Z-ring via a bundling-like mechanism that concentrates and organizes FtsZ polymers.
claims.source: Our genetic, cytological, and biochemical data in sum suggest a model in which Staphylococcal FtsZ begins assembling at mid-cell and recruits GpsB to that location (Figure 7B) where GpsB stabilizes the Z-ring via a bundling-like mechanism that concentrates and organizes FtsZ polymers.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the bundling activity observed in vitro.

claims.claim: GpsB reinforces the faithful and robust assembly of FtsZ at mid-cell at the onset of cell division.
claims.source: We propose that this reinforces the faithful and robust assembly of FtsZ at mid-cell at the onset of cell division and drives an increase in the local concentration of FtsZ, which stimulates its GTPase activity, which is linked to treadmilling- an activity that is likely coincident with the initial membrane constriction that initiates cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: After completion of cytokinesis, GpsB redistributes to the cell periphery and awaits the next round of cell division.
claims.source: After completion of cytokinesis, GpsB redistributes to the cell periphery and awaits the next round of cell division.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy showing dynamic localization.

claims.claim: The dynamic redistribution of GpsB is presumably coincident with a dynamic ability to modulate FtsZ activity and may be dependent on the multimerization state of GpsB.
claims.source: It is tempting to speculate that this dynamic redistribution of GpsB, presumably coincident with a dynamic ability to modulate FtsZ activity, is dependent on the multimerization state of GpsB.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed multimerization states and dynamic localization.

claims.claim: The hexameric and dodecameric populations of purified GpsB could represent the active and inactive forms, respectively, of the protein.
claims.source: In this way, the hexameric and dodecameric populations of purified GpsB could represent the active and inactive forms, respectively, of the protein that may mediate its interaction with FtsZ.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the size exclusion chromatography data and functional differences.

claims.claim: The inactive GpsB-L35S was locked in the dodecameric form and did not exhibit dynamic redistribution from the cell periphery to the cell division site in vivo.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, the inactive GpsBL35S was locked in the dodecameric form and did not exhibit the dynamic redistribution from the cell periphery to the cell division site in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography and microscopy data.

claims.claim: Depletion of EzrA, a known interaction partner of GpsB, also leads to cell enlargement.
claims.source: Interestingly, depletion of a known interaction partner of GpsB, EzrA, also leads to cell enlargement, hinting at a possible collaboration between these two proteins in regulating cell division (Jorge et al., 2011; Steele et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on EzrA.

claims.claim: Several divisome proteins in E. coli and B. subtilis that positively regulate cell division by bundling FtsZ polymers do so via inhibition of FtsZ GTPase activity.
claims.source: Several divisome proteins in E. coli and B. subtilis that positively regulate cell division by bundling FtsZ polymers do so via inhibition of FtsZ GTPase activity (Durand-Heredia et al., 2011; Hale et al., 2011; Lutkenhaus et al., 2012; Mohammadi et al., 2009; Pacheco-Gómez et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2008; Small et al., 2007; Tsang and Bernhardt, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on FtsZ regulators.

claims.claim: FtsZ bundling by GpsB is an intermediate step that increases local FtsZ concentration to stimulate GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: In our model, the seemingly contradictory observation that GpsB stimulates GTP hydrolysis, even though it promotes FtsZ bundling may be explained by the proposition that FtsZ bundling is not the ultimate activity of GpsB. Rather, we envision that FtsZ bundling is an intermediate step that increases local FtsZ concentration to stimulate GTP hydrolysis (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: In E. coli, FtsZ polymers bundled by other proteins require FtsA to disrupt the bundles and destabilize FtsZ polymers.
claims.source: This set of opposing activities exhibited in S. aureus in a single protein is reminiscent of the model in E. coli, where FtsZ polymers bundled by other proteins require a separate protein, FtsA, that can disrupt the bundles and destabilize FtsZ polymers (Conti et al., 2018; Krupka et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on E. coli FtsZ regulation.

claims.claim: FtsZ bundling in B. subtilis requires C-terminal positively charged residues.
claims.source: In a slight variation of this model, since FtsZ bundling in B. subtilis requires C-terminal positively charged residues (Buske and Levin, 2012), it is conceivable that GpsB modulates exposure of the C-terminus of FtsZ to promote FtsZ self-interactions or remodels FtsZ to stabilize a conformation associated with enhanced GTP hydrolysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on B. subtilis FtsZ.

claims.claim: GpsB may orchestrate the organization, stabilization, and activity of FtsZ to remodel the divisome during cell division.
claims.source: In this way, GpsB, an essential S. aureus protein, may orchestrate the organization, stabilization, and activity of FtsZ to remodel the divisome during cell division.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the proposed model.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the context that cell division mechanisms in spherical bacteria are poorly understood compared to rod-shaped bacteria, which have been extensively studied.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C13, and C14 provide well-supported background context from established literature (citations provided) and general scientific consensus. These claims appropriately frame the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

results.result: S. aureus is a significant human pathogen with emerging antibiotic resistance, making bacterial cell division machinery a potential therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are supported by appropriate citations to epidemiological and clinical studies. These claims establish the medical relevance and motivation for studying S. aureus cell division.

results.result: GpsB is a conserved coiled-coil protein in Firmicutes with species-specific functions, typically interacting with peripheral divisome components rather than core machinery, and is essential in S. aureus.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C33 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior structural and functional studies. These claims establish the known properties of GpsB orthologs and set up the contrast with the novel findings in S. aureus.

results.result: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB, but not B. subtilis GpsB, causes severe growth defects and filamentation in B. subtilis, disrupting FtsZ localization independently of peripheral cell division factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C41 are supported by growth assays, microscopy data (Figure 1), immunoblotting, and genetic complementation experiments. The data consistently show species-specific toxicity and demonstrate that the phenotype does not require peripheral divisome components.

results.result: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB in S. aureus causes cell enlargement, while overproduction of B. subtilis GpsB does not, demonstrating species-specific inhibition of cell division.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 and C6 are supported by immunoblotting quantification and microscopy with cell size measurements (Figure 2). The data show ~5.4-fold overproduction and 56.9% of cells exceeding 1.2 μm diameter, with appropriate controls.

results.result: Depletion of GpsB in S. aureus arrests cell division, prevents completion of cytokinesis, and leads to aberrant membrane accumulation and cell lysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C46, C47, and C95 are supported by antisense RNA depletion experiments and time-lapse microscopy (Figure 2L). However, the depletion is only ~2.5-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), which may be incomplete. The phenotypes are clearly documented but the extent of depletion could be more complete.

results.result: The L35S suppressor mutation in GpsB corrects the overproduction growth defect, does not affect secondary structure, but locks the protein in a dodecameric form that fails to localize properly or stimulate FtsZ GTPase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50, C53, C64, C70, C74, and C105 are supported by genetic analysis, CD spectroscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), microscopy (Figures 2I-J, 3A), size exclusion chromatography (Figure 5B), and biochemical assays (Figures 5F, 6A). The data consistently show loss of function associated with altered oligomerization.

results.result: GpsB localizes to the cell periphery in non-dividing cells, relocates to mid-cell at the onset of division forming an irregular ring structure, co-constricts with the division machinery during cytokinesis, and redistributes to the periphery after cell division.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C51, C52, C56-C59, C96, and C102 are supported by extensive microscopy data including epifluorescence, structured illumination microscopy (SIM) (Figure 3B), and time-lapse imaging (Figure 3C). The dynamic localization pattern is well-documented through multiple cell division cycles.

results.result: S. aureus GpsB is not directly membrane-associated, unlike the L. monocytogenes ortholog, as it is detected exclusively in the soluble fraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C54 and C55 are supported by cell fractionation and immunoblotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E). The comparison with L. monocytogenes GpsB and the sequence difference at the membrane-binding residue (Ala23 vs Leu24) provide additional support.

results.result: GpsB localization to mid-cell depends directly or indirectly on functional FtsZ, as demonstrated by FtsZ inhibitor experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by microscopy experiments using the FtsZ inhibitor PC190723 (Figure 4E-F'). In the presence of inhibitor, GpsB fails to localize to mid-cell in all cells observed (n=200), showing clear dependence on FtsZ function.

results.result: Overproduction of GpsB disrupts divisome assembly, while depletion of GpsB prevents robust divisome assembly at mid-cell, as shown by ZapA-GFP localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C62 are supported by microscopy and fluorescence quantification of ZapA-GFP (Figure 4G-K'). The data show 86% mislocalization upon overproduction and ~4-fold reduction in fluorescence intensity upon depletion, with appropriate sample sizes (n=75-200).

results.result: S. aureus GpsB exists in two oligomeric forms, hexameric and dodecameric, as determined by size exclusion chromatography.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by size exclusion chromatography data (Figure 5B) showing two distinct peaks corresponding to predicted hexameric and dodecameric forms. The interpretation is reasonable based on molecular weight standards, though additional methods (e.g., analytical ultracentrifugation, native mass spectrometry) would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: S. aureus FtsZ exhibits poor GTP hydrolysis below ~30 μM and shows concentration-dependent increase in hydrolysis rate, differing from E. coli FtsZ but similar to S. pneumoniae FtsZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C65 and C66 are supported by GTP hydrolysis assays (Figure 5C-D). The data are consistent with a high critical concentration for S. aureus FtsZ. The authors acknowledge discrepancy with one prior study but cite another supporting their findings.

results.result: GpsB stimulates FtsZ GTPase activity in a concentration-dependent manner, with ~3-fold stimulation at 10 μM GpsB and 30 μM FtsZ, while GpsB alone shows no GTPase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69, C10, C71, and C97 are supported by GTP hydrolysis assays (Figure 5E-F). The non-linear stimulation pattern and substoichiometric requirement are well-documented. Controls showing no activity for GpsB alone and no stimulation by GpsB-L35S strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: GpsB directly interacts with polymerized FtsZ, as demonstrated by co-sedimentation assays showing 94% of GpsB pelleting with FtsZ-GMPCPP polymers, while only 20% of GpsB-L35S co-sediments.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 and C7 are supported by ultracentrifugation co-sedimentation assays (Figure 6A). The quantitative differences between wild-type and L35S mutant, along with controls showing GpsB solubility in the absence of FtsZ, provide strong evidence for direct interaction.

results.result: GpsB bundles FtsZ filaments, promoting lateral interactions that increase filament length from ~100 nm to ~1 μm and cause parallel orientation, without requiring GTP hydrolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79, C9, C84, and C98 are supported by differential centrifugation assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and transmission electron microscopy (Figure 6D-E, H-I, and supplement 1C-E). The bundling activity is demonstrated with both GTP and GMPCPP, and the morphological changes are clearly visible.

results.result: Light scattering assays show that GpsB dramatically enhances FtsZ assembly kinetics at 30 μM FtsZ, and the resulting higher-order structures are reversible, disassembling as GTP is depleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by light scattering experiments (Figure 6J-L). The concentration dependence, kinetic enhancement, and reversibility are well-documented. Controls with nucleotide regeneration system (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) confirm that disassembly is linked to GTP depletion.

results.result: The proposed mechanism is that GpsB bundling increases local FtsZ concentration, which triggers GTP hydrolysis, with bundling as an intermediate step rather than the ultimate activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C91, and C108 propose a mechanistic model integrating the bundling and GTPase stimulation activities. While the individual activities are well-supported, the causal relationship (bundling → increased local concentration → GTPase stimulation) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. Additional experiments measuring local FtsZ concentration or testing the model with controlled FtsZ densities would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Intracellular concentrations of FtsZ and GpsB in S. aureus are approximately 28 μM and 10 μM, respectively, corresponding closely to the in vitro reaction conditions used.
results.evaluation: Claims C88 and C89 are supported by citation to proteomics data and personal communication. The calculation from molecule numbers to concentration (C89) is straightforward and appropriate, assuming a cell diameter of 0.8 μm. This provides important physiological context for the biochemical experiments.

results.result: GpsB is proposed to exist as a multimer with 6-12 binding sites, and the hexameric and dodecameric forms may represent active and inactive states, respectively, mediating dynamic localization during the cell cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C103, and C104 are speculative proposals based on the size exclusion chromatography data (C63) and the observation that L35S is locked in dodecameric form and non-functional. While the correlation is suggestive, direct evidence linking oligomeric state to activity or localization dynamics is lacking. The speculation is reasonable but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: S. aureus GpsB uniquely interacts directly with the core divisome component FtsZ, unlike other Firmicutes GpsB orthologs that interact with peripheral components, and is the first reported FtsZ regulator that both bundles filaments and stimulates GTPase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C32, and C92 are supported by the direct interaction data (C7, C73-C75), functional complementation experiments (C41), and comparison with cited literature on other GpsB orthologs (C28-C32). The novelty claim (C92) is reasonable based on cited literature showing other bundling proteins inhibit GTPase activity (C107).

results.result: The proposed model is that GpsB participates in the initial FtsZ treadmilling-dependent step of S. aureus cell division by stabilizing the Z-ring through bundling, increasing local FtsZ concentration, and stimulating GTPase activity to trigger treadmilling and membrane constriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C86, C87, C11, C12, C99-C101, and C111 present an integrated model of GpsB function in vivo. While the model is consistent with the experimental data and cited literature on S. aureus cell division (C86), it remains largely speculative. The localization and biochemical activities are well-supported, but the specific roles in Z-ring stabilization, treadmilling initiation, and divisome remodeling are inferred rather than directly demonstrated. Testing this model would require additional experiments such as measuring FtsZ dynamics in vivo with and without GpsB.

results.result: FtsZ and GpsB concentrations in vivo are poised at the threshold between assembly and disassembly, and overexpression phenotypes are consistent with excessive GTPase activity preventing coordinated FtsZ polymerization and treadmilling.
results.evaluation: Claims C93 and C94 integrate the intracellular concentration data (C88-C89) with the biochemical findings and phenotypic observations. The interpretation that overexpression causes excessive GTPase activity is consistent with the cell enlargement phenotype resembling FtsZ depletion (cited literature). The threshold model is a reasonable interpretation of the data.

results.result: The findings are contextualized by comparison with other bacterial systems: EzrA depletion also causes enlargement, other FtsZ bundling proteins inhibit GTPase activity, E. coli requires FtsA to disrupt bundles, and B. subtilis FtsZ bundling requires C-terminal charged residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C107, C109, and C110 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These comparisons effectively place the S. aureus GpsB findings in the broader context of bacterial cell division mechanisms and highlight the unique properties of the S. aureus system.
